questions.q: Why does this lesson say a demo that only ever shows the approved path undersells Project 3's actual achievement?
options: Approved demos are technically impossible to run live
An agent that only ever gets approved doesn't prove the checkpoint works -- it proves the rejected path, where the real safety value lives, was never tested
Rejected demos are required by the Messages API
There is no meaningful difference between the two outcomes
questions.explain: The whole point of Project 3 is the human-in-the-loop checkpoint. Showing only approvals never demonstrates that the checkpoint actually blocks something -- the rejected path is the proof.

questions.q: What should a demo of the rejected path specifically show, per this lesson?
options: The agent crashing when a tool is rejected
A question that triggers the sensitive tool, the request being rejected live, and Claude's response to the resulting is_error tool_result
Only the final text output with no explanation of what happened
A rejected request that silently disappears with no further response
questions.explain: The rejected-path demo should walk through the real mechanics: the pending approval, the rejection, and Claude's resulting response -- the same is_error pattern built in Lesson 15.

questions.q: Why does this lesson prefer a specific limitations list (e.g., 'no rate limit on approval requests per conversation') over a vague statement like 'could be more secure'?
options: Vague statements are factually incorrect
Specificity is what separates a project that looks thoughtfully built from one that was finished just well enough to demo
The Messages API requires exact wording for limitations sections
Specific limitations are required to pass the lesson's quiz only
questions.explain: A concrete, named gap shows genuine understanding of the system's edges; a vague hedge doesn't demonstrate anything specific about what was actually considered.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three distinct problem shapes do Projects 1-3 together cover?
options: Three different versions of the same RAG pattern
Retrieval (RAG), structured data (SQL/APIs), and action-taking (a tool-using agent with approval)
Frontend, backend, and database administration
Three unrelated topics with no common theme
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the three projects as a deliberately varied portfolio: retrieval, structured data work, and action-taking -- covering the kinds of AI application work most hiring managers actually see.

questions.q: What comes immediately after this lesson, per the course outline?
options: Chapter 5, Career Preparation
Chapter 1, Capstone Overview
Lesson 13, Project 3 Kickoff
The course ends here with no further chapters
questions.explain: Lesson 18 closes Chapter 4 (Project 3) and the three-project sequence; Chapter 5, Career Preparation, is the final chapter, turning the projects into a resume and interview answers.
